title: First Gastroenterologist Appointment: What to Expect for IBS or IBD
summary: Know what your first GI visit involves and walk in prepared.
body_markdown:
A first gastroenterologist appointment is mostly a detailed conversation about your gut, followed by a short physical exam and a plan for any tests. Many people arrive with ongoing diarrhea, constipation, belly pain, bloating or bleeding and one question: is this irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) or inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), the group that includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis? This guide walks through the visit in order, answers the awkward questions and explains how to prepare a one-page summary.


## What happens at a first gastroenterology appointment


The gastroenterologist takes your history, examines you and then explains which tests, if any, they recommend. The[National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) describes this sequence for IBS](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/irritable-bowel-syndrome/diagnosis) : a review of symptoms and medical and family history, then a physical exam. Expect to leave with a working impression and a plan. Conditions such as IBD are confirmed by tests done later.


Plan for more time than the consultation itself. The gastroenterology division at Weill Cornell Medicine, for example,[asks new patients to arrive 30 minutes early and to expect up to 2 hours at the office](https://medicine.weill.cornell.edu/sites/default/files/new_patient_packet.pdf) . Practices differ, so your own confirmation is the better guide.


Scope procedures generally need their own appointment. A colonoscopy[involves a laxative bowel prep, sometimes a clear-liquid diet for a day or more, and sedation, so you need a ride home afterward](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diagnostic-tests/colonoscopy) . Because of that preparation, a first consultation usually ends with a plan and a date for any procedure.


## The questions your gastroenterologist will ask


Expect questions about when symptoms started and how they have changed, how many bowel movements you have a day, what the stool looks like, whether you see blood or mucus, whether symptoms wake you at night and whether you have lost weight without trying. These details steer the workup, because[NIDDK lists anemia, rectal bleeding, black and tarry stools and weight loss](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/irritable-bowel-syndrome/diagnosis) as symptoms that may point to a condition other than IBS.


The doctor will also ask about medicines, recent infections, stressful events around the time symptoms began, your diet and your other health problems, all part of[NIDDK's description of the IBS history](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/irritable-bowel-syndrome/diagnosis) . Mention over-the-counter pain relievers, laxatives, antidiarrheal products, vitamins and herbal supplements as well as prescriptions.


Family history carries weight. Doctors ask specifically about relatives with[celiac disease, colon cancer or inflammatory bowel disease](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/irritable-bowel-syndrome/diagnosis) . If you are unsure, check with a parent or sibling before the appointment.


## The physical exam, including whether a rectal exam is likely


The exam centers on your abdomen. The doctor usually[checks for bloating, listens with a stethoscope and taps on the abdomen to find tenderness or pain](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/irritable-bowel-syndrome/diagnosis) . When Crohn's disease is possible, the exam may widen to a[full-body check for weight loss and inflammation in other parts of the body](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/crohns-disease/diagnosis) .


Whether you have a digital rectal exam, in which the clinician inserts a gloved, lubricated finger into the rectum, depends on your symptoms. Cleveland Clinic lists[rectal bleeding, blood in the stool, constipation or diarrhea, and fecal incontinence](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diagnostics/24212-digital-rectal-exam) among the reasons for one, and it can help evaluate hemorrhoids, anal fissures and IBD. When ulcerative colitis is suspected, the[physical exam may include a rectal exam to check for blood in the stool](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/ulcerative-colitis/diagnosis) .


The exam[only takes a few minutes and is typically painless, though it may feel slightly uncomfortable](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diagnostics/24212-digital-rectal-exam) . Tell the doctor first if you have hemorrhoids or a tear in the anal skin. You can ask why the exam is recommended and what it will check. You can also ask for a chaperone, and the[American Medical Association's Code of Medical Ethics](https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-chaperones) says physicians should always honor that request.


## Tests you may be sent for next


Testing is selective. For suspected IBS,[NIDDK notes that doctors usually do not need tests to make the diagnosis](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/irritable-bowel-syndrome/diagnosis) . Blood and stool tests mainly check for anemia, infection, blood or other disease.


Two tests come up often when diarrhea is part of the picture. The[American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) IBS guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33315591/) suggests a blood test for celiac disease and a fecal calprotectin test, a stool marker of intestinal inflammation, for people with suspected IBS and diarrhea. A high calprotectin result points toward inflammation, but it does not diagnose IBD on its own, because[ulcerative colitis is diagnosed with endoscopy and biopsies](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/ulcerative-colitis/diagnosis) .


A colonoscopy can[check for conditions such as colon cancer or IBD](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/irritable-bowel-syndrome/diagnosis) , and an upper endoscopy with biopsy can check for celiac disease. ACG[recommends against routine colonoscopy for people with IBS symptoms under 45 who have no warning signs](https://webfiles.gi.org/docs/publications/ibs_guideline_acg_magazine.pdf) , such as unintentional weight loss, symptoms that start at an older age or a family history of IBD or colon cancer. For suspected Crohn's disease,[endoscopy is the most accurate test](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/crohns-disease/diagnosis) , and CT or MRI scans may be added.


## How to prepare: eating, clothing and what to bring


Follow any eating or drinking instructions on your confirmation, and call the clinic if a same-day blood draw or procedure is possible. If you take prescription medicines, including any IBD medicines, ask the clinic when you book whether to take them as usual on the day of your visit. If celiac disease is a possibility, hold off on going gluten-free, because starting the diet before testing[can affect test results](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/celiac-disease/diagnosis) . Wear comfortable clothing that is easy to adjust for an abdominal exam.


Weill Cornell, for instance, asks new patients to bring[insurance cards, referrals, photo identification and a list of medicines that includes herbal supplements and vitamins](https://medicine.weill.cornell.edu/sites/default/files/new_patient_packet.pdf) , to send prior lab, pathology, radiology and procedure reports ahead of time, and asks for full payment at the visit from patients without insurance cards or proper referrals. Check whether your plan needs a referral on file.


A one-page summary makes your account easier to act on. Use dates wherever you can, in three blocks:


- Symptoms: when they started, what has changed, and a two-week record of stool frequency, form, blood, pain and nighttime symptoms.
- History: every medicine with dose and how often you take it, recent infections or travel, and relevant family history.
- Your top three questions, in priority order, with space for answers.


If you already have IBD and are seeing a new gastroenterologist, add recent endoscopy, pathology and lab reports and past treatments with why each stopped. Hand a copy to the nurse at check-in. Do not wait for the appointment if you develop[stools that contain red blood or are black and tarry, severe abdominal or rectal pain, a high fever or signs of dehydration](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/diarrhea/symptoms-causes) ; contact a doctor right away.


## If IBS or IBD is suspected


The[ACG guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33315591/) favors a positive, symptom-based IBS diagnosis with limited testing, which shortens the time to treatment. The current standard is Rome V, which was[published in 2026](https://news.gastro.org/issues/2026/august-2026/rome-v-criteria-capture-more-people-with-ibs-but-a-milder-group/) . The[Rome V criteria](https://theromefoundation.org/rome-v-criteria/) describe recurrent, but not continuous, abdominal pain or discomfort on average at least 3 days per month over the last 3 months, linked to at least two of three features: a connection to bowel movements, a change in stool frequency or a change in stool form, with symptoms starting at least 6 months before diagnosis. Some older pages still show a once-a-week threshold from the previous Rome IV version. For more, see[IBS vs IBD: key differences, red flags and the tests doctors use](https://aidyhq.com/learn/ibs-vs-ibd-key-differences-red-flags-and-the-tests-doctors-use) .


When IBD is suspected, the next weeks usually involve blood and stool tests followed by endoscopy. For a colonoscopy,[biopsy results can take days or longer](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diagnostic-tests/colonoscopy) . If IBD is confirmed, you may want to[find an IBD specialist](https://aidyhq.com/learn/how-to-find-an-ibd-specialist-not-just-a-general-gastroenterologist) and learn[what happens at your first IBD follow-up appointment](https://aidyhq.com/learn/what-happens-at-your-first-ibd-follow-up-appointment) .


## Questions to ask before you leave


Five questions cover most first visits. Ask what the doctor thinks is most likely and what else they want to rule out. Ask which tests they are ordering and what each one will show. Ask how and when you will get results, and who to contact if you have not heard back. Ask whether you should change anything about your diet, medicines or daily routine while you wait. Finally, ask which symptoms should prompt a call or an urgent visit before the next appointment.


Write the answers down or bring someone who can take notes. A first gastroenterology appointment sets the direction for everything that follows. Dated symptoms, a complete medicine list and your outside records help the doctor choose the right tests, and these questions help you leave knowing what happens next and when to seek care sooner.


This article is for educational purposes and is not medical advice. It is researched against current AGA clinical guidelines and peer-reviewed sources. Always discuss treatment decisions with your care team.
